title: Ulm to Princeton: the Patent Clerk Who Bent Light and Time
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Ulm, Munich, and the Needle of the Compass

stops.name: Ulm, the house on the Bahnhofstraße
stops.campa: Albert is born at half past eleven on a Friday morning in a rented apartment on the Bahnhofstraße, the second child expected of Hermann Einstein, an featherbed-and-electrical salesman, and his wife Pauline, born Koch. His mother, seeing the newborn's oddly angular, heavy-looking head, is at first frightened that something is wrong with him; the midwife and doctors reassure her it will round out, and it does. Within a year the family leaves Ulm for Munich, where Hermann and his brother Jakob will found an electrical engineering works. Ulm itself he barely knows; he returns to it only in memory.
suggested_refs: The plaque at Bahnhofstraße 20, Ulm, marking the house of Einstein's birth (destroyed in the Second World War)
sources: Einstein Papers Project, Vol. 1, biographical note
Walter Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe (2007)
Albrecht Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography (1997)

stops.name: Munich, the compass in the sickbed
stops.campa: Sick in bed at four or five years old in the family's Munich apartment, Albert is given a pocket compass by his father to amuse him. He turns it in his hands and watches the needle swing back always to the same unseen north, indifferent to how he twists the case, obeying a force his eyes cannot find in the room at all. The ordinary objects of his childhood, thrown balls, blown bubbles, have always seemed to him to have direct, tangible causes; this needle answers to nothing he can see or touch, and the strangeness of it lodges in him and does not leave.
stops.quote: I can still remember — or at least believe I can remember — that this experience made a deep and lasting impression upon me. Something deeply hidden had to be behind things.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical Notes (1949)
suggested_refs: The pocket compass shown to the sick child, the founding relic of the Einstein legend
sources: Albert Einstein, Autobiographical Notes (1949)
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Abraham Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...' (1982)

stops.name: Munich, the sacred geometry booklet and the break with the Church
stops.campa: At twelve, a poor Jewish medical student named Max Talmud (later Talmey), a Thursday dinner guest of the Einsteins for years, puts into Albert's hands a little book of Euclidean plane geometry. He works through it alone that summer, calling it ever after his holy geometry booklet, astonished that a claim like the intersection of a triangle's altitudes could be proven with such certainty from bare axioms. The same season, reading the popular science volumes Talmud also brings him, he concludes that much of the Bible's history cannot be literally true, and the devout, ardent faith of his early boyhood falls away into a fierce, private freethinking.
stops.quote: Through the reading of popular scientific books I soon reached the conviction that much in the stories of the Bible could not be true... the consequence was a positively fanatic freethinking.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical Notes (1949)
suggested_refs: Max Talmey's gift copy of the Euclidean geometry textbook, the 'holy little geometry book'
sources: Autobiographical Notes (1949)
Max Talmey, The Relativity Theory Simplified (1932), reminiscences
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Munich, the Luitpold Gymnasium and the family's departure
stops.campa: The Einstein electrical works fails to win the contract to light Munich and the family's fortunes collapse; in the summer of 1894 Hermann, Pauline, and Albert's sister Maja move to Pavia in northern Italy to try again, leaving sixteen-year-old Albert behind in Munich to finish his schooling at the Luitpold Gymnasium, boarding with a relative. He hates the school's rote drilling and military rigidity, is warned by a teacher that his mere presence undermines the class's respect, and before the year is out a doctor's certificate of nervous exhaustion, and his own restlessness, send him after his family into Italy without a diploma.
stops.quote: It is, in fact, nothing short of a miracle that the modern methods of instruction have not yet entirely strangled the holy curiosity of inquiry.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical Notes (1949)
suggested_refs: The Luitpold Gymnasium building on Müllerstraße, Munich, where Einstein was a reluctant pupil
sources: Autobiographical Notes (1949)
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Zurich, the failed entrance examination
stops.campa: Two years under the required age, Albert sits the entrance examination for the Federal Polytechnic in Zurich, urged on by a family friend who believes in him. He shines in the mathematics and physics papers, outscoring the examiners' expectations, but fails outright in French, botany, and politics, and is refused admission. The principal, Albin Herzog, impressed nonetheless, advises him not to retreat to Munich but to finish his schooling properly at the cantonal school in Aarau and reapply in a year without the exam. Wounded but not broken, Albert takes the advice, and Aarau, not Zurich, becomes the gate he actually walks through.
suggested_refs: The Federal Polytechnic (later ETH Zürich) building on the Rämistrasse, site of the failed and later passed examinations
sources: Einstein Papers Project, Vol. 1
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Aarau, the Kantonsschule and the essay on the future
stops.campa: Boarding a happy year with the family of his teacher Jost Winteler in Aarau, Albert finishes his schooling in the freer, more humane Swiss system he will praise for the rest of his life, and in January renounces his German citizenship to become, for five years, a man without a country. For a French class assignment he writes 'Mes projets d'avenir,' setting down plainly the plan of study in mathematics and physics at Zurich that he means to follow, and the ambition, already, to become a teacher of theoretical science. In September he takes his matura and passes; the road to the Polytechnic opens.
stops.quote: If I have the good fortune to pass my examinations, I would go to Zurich. I would stay there for four years to study mathematics and physics. I imagine myself becoming a teacher in those branches of natural science, choosing the theoretical part of them.
stops.quote_source: School essay, 'Mes projets d'avenir,' Aarau, 18 September 1896
suggested_refs: The manuscript of 'Mes projets d'avenir,' Einstein's schoolboy French essay, Aarau Kantonsschule archive
sources: Einstein Papers Project, Vol. 1, Doc. 22
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Zurich, the Polytechnic and Mileva Marić
stops.campa: Albert enters the mathematics and physics teaching diploma course at the Federal Polytechnic, one of five students in Section VI A, and the only woman among them is Mileva Marić, a Serbian from Novi Sad who has crossed half of Europe against convention to study physics. He skips lectures he finds dull, in particular Hermann Minkowski's, working instead from Kirchhoff and Helmholtz in his rented room, and it is Marcel Grossmann's careful lecture notes that carry him through the exams each spring. Between Albert and Mileva a courtship of shared physics and long, searching letters begins that will outlast the Polytechnic itself.
stops.quote: I need my Dollie for building up my little theories much more than she needs me. I feel so alone... but this loneliness [is nothing] compared with the way I felt before I knew her.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Mileva Marić, 1900
suggested_refs: The main building of the Eidgenössische Polytechnische Schule (ETH Zürich) on the Rämistrasse
sources: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 1
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Zurich, graduation and the wilderness of unemployment
stops.campa: Einstein graduates in August 1900 with the diploma to teach mathematics and physics, but of the four graduates in his class he alone is left without a post; he believes, and later insists, that his physics professor Heinrich Weber has quietly blackballed him among academic contacts for his independence and his skipped lectures. For nearly two years he scrapes by on tutoring jobs and short substitute-teaching posts in Winterthur and Schaffhausen, applying by postcard to laboratories across Europe and hearing nothing back, while Mileva, still working toward her own diploma, twice fails the final examination that would have made her a physicist in her own right.
stops.quote: I would have found employment long ago if Weber had not played a double game with me.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Mileva Marić, 1901
suggested_refs: Einstein's 1900 Polytechnic diploma in mathematics and physics teaching
sources: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 1
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Novi Sad, the birth of Lieserl
stops.campa: Unmarried and apart from Albert, who is job-hunting in Switzerland, Mileva returns to her parents' house in Novi Sad to bear their daughter in January 1902, a girl the letters call Lieserl. Albert, still awaiting word, writes anxiously asking after the baby's health and eyes, and says he loves her already though he has not seen her. After this single winter the child disappears from every surviving letter and record: whether she was given up for adoption, died of scarlet fever, or was cared for by Mileva's family is never afterward set down by either parent, and the mystery of Lieserl closes over itself for good.
stops.quote: Is she healthy, and does she already cry properly to make her lungs strong? What kind of eyes does she have? Which one of us does she resemble more?
stops.quote_source: Letter to Mileva Marić, 1902
suggested_refs: The surviving Einstein–Marić love letters (published 1987), sole record of Lieserl's existence
sources: The Love Letters of Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić (ed. Renn & Schulmann, 1992)
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Bern, the post at the patent office
stops.campa: On his friend Marcel Grossmann's recommendation, Einstein is hired as a technical expert third class at the Federal Office for Intellectual Property in Bern, examining patent applications for electrical devices at a salary that at last lets him think of marriage. He takes a room on the corner of Speichergasse and Genfergasse, across from the clock tower whose bells will later help him picture two observers disagreeing about simultaneity. The work suits him: orderly, well-paid, undemanding enough to leave his mind free, so that within it, in the evenings and on his walks home, the shape of a whole new physics begins to gather.
stops.quote: That worldly cloister where I hatched my most beautiful ideas.
stops.quote_source: Recollection of the Bern patent office, as recorded by colleagues and biographers
suggested_refs: The Federal Office for Intellectual Property building, corner of Speichergasse and Genfergasse, Bern
sources: Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property (IGE), 'Einstein at the Patent Office'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Bern, the Olympia Academy
stops.campa: In rooms he shares with his young friends Conrad Habicht and Maurice Solovine, Einstein founds, half in jest and wholly in earnest, the Akademie Olympia: three young men reading Hume, Mach, Poincaré, and Spinoza aloud over bread, cheese, and sausage late into the night, and arguing until the arguments turn to laughter. It is an academy with no professors, no doctrine, and no members but themselves, and Einstein will look back on it for the rest of his life as the true seedbed of his physics, more formative than any lecture hall he ever sat in as a student.
stops.quote: The Olympia Academy, in its glorious and dignified inactivity, still lights up our lonely lives from time to time with its cheerful eye.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Maurice Solovine, 1953
suggested_refs: Maurice Solovine's memoir of the Olympia Academy meetings in Bern
sources: Maurice Solovine, Albert Einstein: Letters to Solovine
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Bern, the marriage to Mileva
stops.campa: With only Habicht and Solovine as witnesses, Albert and Mileva marry in a brief civil ceremony in Bern; his mother Pauline, who considers Mileva too old and too much a physicist for her son, does not attend and does not forgive it for years. That night, the story runs, Einstein returns home from the small wedding dinner to find he has forgotten his key, and wakes his landlady rather than his bride to let him in. The household that forms in the Kramgasse apartment above a delicatessen is a working household of two physicists, Mileva keeping the accounts of a marriage that will carry the annus mirabilis within two years.
suggested_refs: The apartment at Kramgasse 49, Bern, where the young couple lived and Einstein worked in 1905
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Bern, the light-quanta of March
stops.campa: Working evenings after his patent-office day, Einstein completes 'On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light,' proposing that light itself, however wave-like on the whole, arrives and is absorbed in discrete quanta of energy, not a continuous flood. It is the boldest paper of that year and the one he himself will call revolutionary; it explains the stubborn oddities of the photoelectric effect that classical wave theory cannot touch, and though almost no one accepts it at first, not even Planck, whose own quantum idea it extends, it is this paper, not relativity, for which Stockholm will one day give him the Nobel Prize.
stops.quote: According to the assumption to be contemplated here, when a light ray is spreading from a point, the energy is not distributed continuously over ever-increasing spaces, but consists of a finite number of energy quanta.
stops.quote_source: 'On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light,' Annalen der Physik, 1905
suggested_refs: The 1905 photoelectric-effect paper, later cited for the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
sources: Annalen der Physik 17 (1905)
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Bern, the doctorate and the dance of the pollen grains
stops.campa: In the same burst of months Einstein finishes a doctoral dissertation determining molecular dimensions from the viscosity of sugar solutions, which the University of Zurich will accept, and a second paper explaining the jittering, random dance of pollen grains suspended in water, first noticed by the botanist Robert Brown eight decades before, as the visible fingerprint of the ceaseless bombardment of unseen molecules. Where philosophers still doubt whether atoms are anything more than a convenient fiction, Einstein gives a number that can be checked with a microscope and a stopwatch, and within a few years the last skeptics of atomic reality, Ostwald among them, concede the case is closed.
stops.quote: If the movement discussed here can actually be observed... then classical thermodynamics can no longer be looked upon as applicable with precision to bodies even of dimensions distinguishable in a microscope.
stops.quote_source: 'On the Movement of Small Particles Suspended in Stationary Liquids,' Annalen der Physik, 1905
suggested_refs: Jean Perrin's later microscope confirmations of Einstein's Brownian-motion formula (1908–1909)
sources: Annalen der Physik 17 (1905)
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'

stops.name: Bern, the electrodynamics of moving bodies
stops.campa: Einstein submits 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,' known ever after as the founding paper of special relativity, though the word relativity appears nowhere prominent in its title. From two plain postulates, that physics looks the same to any observer moving at constant speed, and that light travels at one speed for all of them regardless of their own motion, he derives that time runs differently for observers in relative motion, that lengths contract, that simultaneity is not absolute. He needs no laboratory for it, only the clock tower he passes daily on his way to the patent office, and the discipline to follow the postulates wherever they lead.
stops.quote: The introduction of a 'luminiferous ether' will prove to be superfluous inasmuch as the view here to be developed will not require an 'absolutely stationary space.'
stops.quote_source: 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,' Annalen der Physik, 1905
suggested_refs: The Bern clock tower (Zytglogge), cited in Einstein's own recollections of the thought-experiments behind special relativity
sources: Annalen der Physik 17 (1905)
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Bern, does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy content
stops.campa: As an afterthought to the relativity paper, barely three pages long, Einstein works out that a body which radiates energy loses mass in exact proportion, and states the relation that will outlive every other sentence he writes: mass and energy are the same quantity measured two ways, mass merely a very concentrated store of energy, convertible in principle at the rate of the speed of light squared. He signs it still as a patent examiner, uncelebrated, in a Bern rented room; four papers in seven months, the photon, the atom's proof, the relativity of time, and this equivalence, remake physics from a desk that is not even a university's.
stops.quote: The mass of a body is a measure of its energy content.
stops.quote_source: 'Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?', Annalen der Physik, 1905
suggested_refs: E = mc², the equation of mass-energy equivalence, first stated in this 1905 note
sources: Annalen der Physik 18 (1905)
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Zurich, professor at the university
stops.campa: Four years after the miracle year, still slow to be recognized outside a small circle of physicists who write to him, Einstein is at last offered a chair, associate professor of theoretical physics at the University of Zurich, and leaves the patent office he has loved for its quiet. To Jakob Laub he jokes darkly about trading independence for academic rank; the pay, at first, is actually less than the patent office gave him, though the honor is greater. His students find him informal, unpretentious, given to interrupting his own lectures with, 'wait a moment, I have to think this over again', a habit no professor before him had ever risked in front of a class.
stops.quote: So, now I too am an official member of the guild of whores.
stops.quote_source: Letter to a colleague on accepting the Zurich professorship, 1909
suggested_refs: The University of Zurich, Einstein's first academic chair after seven years at the patent office
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Prague, the German University
stops.campa: A full professorship, better paid and more prestigious, draws the family to Prague and the German half of its divided university, where Einstein becomes, for the Austro-Hungarian bureaucracy's records, a subject required to declare a religion, and chooses, indifferently, 'mosaic.' He finds Prague society stiff with rank and small vanities that amuse him more than they trouble him, and works at the Institute for Theoretical Physics on the gravitational bending of starlight, publishing in 1911 the first, still-incomplete prediction that a ray grazing the sun should be deflected, a number later observers will need to correct, but the germ of the theory that will make him famous is already showing itself here.
suggested_refs: The Institute for Theoretical Physics of the German University, Viničná Street, Prague, where Einstein first calculated light-bending by gravity
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Brussels, the first Solvay Congress
stops.campa: Invited among the twenty-odd physicists Ernest Solvay gathers at the Hotel Metropole to argue out the crisis of the quantum, Einstein meets Marie Curie, Henri Poincaré, Max Planck, and Ernest Rutherford in one room for the first time, the youngest man there apart from a handful. He finds the proceedings, for all the illustrious names, oddly barren of real progress, a lament over the old physics's wreck rather than a plan for the new. Walking the corridors between sessions, he and Curie begin a friendship of mutual respect that lasts the rest of her life, two of the few unafraid to say plainly what they do not yet understand.
stops.quote: The Solvay Congress was on the whole a lamentation over the ruins of Jeans' theory. Nothing positive came out of it.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Heinrich Zangger, November 1911
suggested_refs: The 1911 Solvay Congress photograph, the first gathering of the modern quantum physicists
sources: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 5
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Zurich, the return to the Polytechnic and Grossmann's tensors
stops.campa: Called back to Zurich, now as a full professor of the very Polytechnic that once made him wait a year to enter, Einstein turns in earnest to generalizing relativity to gravitation and accelerated motion, and finds the mathematics of curved space beyond what he was taught as a student. He appeals to his old classmate Marcel Grossmann, now a professor of mathematics, who introduces him to the tensor calculus of Riemann, Ricci, and Levi-Civita; the two co-author, in 1913, a first joint attempt at the field equations, still flawed, still years from the final form, but the mathematical language of general relativity is set from this collaboration onward.
stops.quote: Grossmann, you must help me, or I'll go crazy!
stops.quote_source: Letter to Marcel Grossmann, 1912
suggested_refs: The 1913 'Entwurf' (outline) theory of gravitation, co-authored with Marcel Grossmann
sources: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 4
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Berlin, the call of the Prussian Academy
stops.campa: Max Planck and Walther Nernst travel to Zurich to persuade Einstein in person, and the offer they bring is unmatched: a salaried seat in the Prussian Academy of Sciences with no teaching duties at all, a research directorship, and a professorship at Berlin University he need only occasionally exercise. He accepts, arriving in Berlin in the spring of 1914 into the most prestigious scientific establishment in the German-speaking world, and into a marriage already failing; within months Mileva and their two sons return to Zurich, leaving Einstein alone in Berlin as Europe slides, that same summer, into general war.
suggested_refs: The Prussian Academy of Sciences building on Unter den Linden, Berlin
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Berlin, the Manifesto to Europeans
stops.campa: When ninety-three of Germany's most eminent intellectuals sign a manifesto defending the war and denying German atrocities in Belgium, Einstein refuses, and instead puts his name, one of only four, to Georg Nicolai's counter-manifesto, the 'Aufruf an die Europäer,' calling on the educated of Europe to unite above the trenches rather than cheer them on. It is a nearly friendless position in wartime Berlin, and it will cost him socially for years, but it marks, publicly and for the first time, the pacifism and internationalism that will run beside the physics for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: Never before has any war so completely destroyed the fabric of international cooperation... it is a duty for educated, internationally minded Europeans at least to attempt to prevent Europe from suffering, as a result of this war, a fate similar to that which befell ancient Greece.
stops.quote_source: Manifesto to Europeans (Aufruf an die Europäer), October 1914
suggested_refs: The 'Aufruf an die Europäer,' Georg Nicolai's pacifist counter-manifesto, one of only four signatures
sources: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 6
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Berlin, the field equations of November
stops.campa: Across four Thursday lectures to the Prussian Academy in November 1915, racing a rival calculation by the mathematician David Hilbert, Einstein corrects and finally completes the field equations of general relativity, the mathematics that ties the shape of space and time to the mass and energy within it. In the same days he applies the still-wet theory to a fifty-year puzzle, the small stubborn drift of Mercury's orbit that Newton's gravity cannot explain, and the new equations account for it exactly, to the decimal. He tells a colleague the discovery gave him heart palpitations; for days, he says, he could not work.
stops.quote: For a few days I was beside myself with joyous excitement.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Arnold Sommerfeld, describing the Mercury calculation, December 1915
suggested_refs: 'The Field Equations of Gravitation,' presented to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, 25 November 1915
sources: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 6
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Berlin, illness, divorce, and the marriage to Elsa
stops.campa: Worn down by wartime shortages and the strain of the theory, Einstein falls seriously ill in 1917 with stomach ailments that will trouble him for years, and is nursed back by his cousin Elsa Löwenthal, in whose Berlin apartment on the Haberlandstraße he has increasingly lived. His divorce from Mileva, agreed with brutal frankness, settles on her the money of a Nobel Prize he has not yet won but is already confident will come; weeks after the decree he marries Elsa, a companionable, undemanding match very unlike the partnership of physics that Mileva's had been.
suggested_refs: The 1919 divorce settlement pledging Einstein's future Nobel Prize money to Mileva Marić and their sons
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: Berlin, the eclipse confirms the theory
stops.campa: Word reaches Einstein in Berlin that at a joint meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society in London, Arthur Eddington has presented photographs taken during the May solar eclipse from Príncipe and Sobral: starlight grazing the darkened sun is bent by exactly the angle general relativity predicts, twice Newton's older figure. The Times calls it a revolution in science; overnight the forty-year-old Berlin professor becomes the most famous scientist alive, mobbed by reporters and photographers in a defeated, hungry Germany that seizes on him as its one undisputed genius. Asked afterward what he would have thought had the eclipse not confirmed the theory, his answer is unhurried.
stops.quote: Then I would have been sorry for the dear Lord. The theory is correct anyway.
stops.quote_source: Recorded by Ilse Rosenthal-Schneider, a student present when the eclipse telegram arrived
suggested_refs: Eddington's 1919 eclipse photographic plates from Príncipe, and the Illustrated London News diagram of the light-bending measurement
sources: Royal Society, Notes and Records (2020), 'The 1919 eclipse results'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'

segments.name: The World Made Small: Nobel, Japan, Jerusalem

stops.name: Princeton and New York, the first American tour
stops.campa: Traveling with Chaim Weizmann to raise funds and support for the Hebrew University planned for Jerusalem, Einstein crosses to America for the first time and finds himself besieged as a celebrity he never sought, crowds at the pier, ticker tape, reporters demanding the theory of relativity explained in one sentence. At Princeton he lectures for four days on relativity to packed halls and receives an honorary doctorate; the university's president jokes that Einstein has raised the intellectual level of the town, at least for the week, considerably above its usual altitude. He finds American publicity exhausting and American generosity, to the Zionist cause he has come to serve, real.
suggested_refs: Einstein's 1921 Princeton lectures, published as The Meaning of Relativity
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 12

stops.name: Japan, the lecture tour and the Nobel telegram
stops.campa: Sailing east for a six-week lecture tour of Japan already arranged months before, Einstein learns aboard ship, by telegram relayed through Shanghai, that the Swedish Academy has awarded him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, specifically and pointedly for the photoelectric-effect paper of 1905, not for relativity, whose confirmation the citation still calls unresolved. He cannot reach Stockholm for the December ceremony without abandoning the Japanese public who have crowded stations and lecture halls to see him, and simply continues on; in Kyoto weeks later, he gives an impromptu, unrecorded-until-transcribed account of how the theory of relativity first came to him, the closest thing to a Nobel lecture the prize will ever get.
stops.quote: I thought of this problem in my mind, considering ways of reforming Newton's mechanics with the Maxwell-Lorentz equations for empty space.
stops.quote_source: 'How I Created the Theory of Relativity,' Kyoto address, December 1922 (recorded by Jun Ishiwara)
suggested_refs: Jun Ishiwara's transcript of the Kyoto lecture, the nearest surviving record of Einstein's own account of discovering relativity
sources: Physics Today, translation of the Kyoto address
Nobel Prize in Physics 1921, official records
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Jerusalem, the first lecture on Mount Scopus
stops.campa: On the same world tour, Einstein and Elsa reach Palestine, where he is received as the great champion of the still-unbuilt Hebrew University. On Mount Scopus, on the site where the university will open two years later, he delivers the first scientific lecture ever given there, opening in Hebrew, a language he does not speak, before continuing his account of relativity in French. Watching Jewish farmers, students, and laborers gathered on the hillside above Jerusalem, he calls it the greatest day of his life, moved less by the physics than by the sight of a scattered people beginning, in this one place, to stand up straight.
stops.quote: I consider this the greatest day of my life. Today I have been made happy by the sight of the Jewish people learning to recognize themselves and to make themselves recognized as a force in the world.
stops.quote_source: Address on Mount Scopus, Jerusalem, 7 February 1923
suggested_refs: Mount Scopus, site of Einstein's 1923 lecture and of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, opened 1925
sources: Jewish Telegraphic Agency archive, 1923
The Forward, '100 years ago, Albert Einstein took his one and only trip to Palestine'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Madrid, the honors of Spain
stops.campa: From Palestine the tour continues to Spain, where King Alfonso XIII receives him and the Royal Spanish Academy of Sciences elects him a corresponding member; he lectures in Madrid and Barcelona to overflowing halls of scientists who have followed the eclipse news in the Spanish press with the same excitement as the rest of Europe. He is fêted, photographed, and made to sit through more banquets than physics colloquia, a pattern of the whole five-and-a-half-month circuit of the globe he undertakes rather than sit in Stockholm for a medal: fame, in these months, running well ahead of any laboratory.
suggested_refs: Einstein's 1923 diary of the journey through the Far East, Palestine, and Spain
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 13

segments.name: Berlin Between the Wars: Quantum Debates and Gathering Shadow

stops.name: Brussels, the debates with Bohr
stops.campa: At the fifth Solvay Congress, devoted to the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Schrödinger, and Born, Einstein rises after each session to propose ingenious thought experiments meant to show that the theory's fundamental uncertainty must be an illusion, a sign of the theory's incompleteness rather than nature's true character; each night Niels Bohr works out, by breakfast, exactly where Einstein's experiment secretly smuggles in the uncertainty it claims to escape. The exchange, courteous and utterly serious on both sides, becomes the defining argument of twentieth-century physics, Einstein insisting to the end of his life that God does not play dice, Bohr replying only that Einstein should stop telling God what to do.
stops.quote: Quantum mechanics is certainly imposing. But an inner voice tells me that it is not yet the real thing... I, at any rate, am convinced that He does not play dice.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Max Born, December 1926, restated through the Solvay debates with Niels Bohr, 1927
suggested_refs: The 1927 Solvay Conference photograph, gathering Einstein, Bohr, Curie, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, and Dirac in one room
sources: The Born-Einstein Letters (1971)
Niels Bohr, 'Discussion with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics' (1949)
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'

stops.name: Pasadena, the winters at Caltech
stops.campa: Three winters running Einstein and Elsa cross to Pasadena as guests of the California Institute of Technology, where he tours the Mount Wilson Observatory with Edwin Hubble, whose measurements of a receding universe of galaxies persuade Einstein at last to abandon the cosmological constant he once inserted, against his own instinct, to keep the universe static. Hollywood claims him too: Charlie Chaplin invites him to the premiere of City Lights, and the two men, walking in together to a roaring, cheering crowd, exchange a joke about which of them the public actually understands. Einstein calls himself, half-amused and half-weary, a kind of scientific prize ox led from banquet to banquet.
suggested_refs: The 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson Observatory, where Einstein reviewed Hubble's evidence for cosmic expansion
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Caltech Archives, Einstein correspondence

stops.name: Caputh, the letter to Freud and the last summer in Germany
stops.campa: At his wooden summer house in Caputh, built with his Nobel money and his one true retreat from Berlin's crowds, Einstein writes at the League of Nations' invitation to Sigmund Freud in Vienna, asking whether the human mind can ever be freed from the pull toward war; Freud's answer, when it comes, is measured and without much comfort. That December, sailing again for Caltech, Einstein tells Elsa, only half in jest, to look hard at their villa, for she will not see it again; within two months Hitler is chancellor of Germany, and the guess proves exact.
stops.quote: Is there any way of delivering mankind from the menace of war? ... This is the problem which you, with your deep insight into the human psyche, may be able to solve.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Sigmund Freud, 'Why War?', 30 July 1932
suggested_refs: The Caputh summer house near Potsdam, and the published Einstein–Freud correspondence, 'Why War?' (1933)
sources: Einstein and Freud, Why War? (League of Nations, 1933)
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Le Coq-sur-Mer, the renunciation of Germany
stops.campa: Hitler is named chancellor while Einstein is still in America; he does not sail home. From a rented villa at the Belgian seaside resort of Le Coq-sur-Mer, guarded now by police against threats on his life and a price rumored on his head, he resigns his seat in the Prussian Academy of Sciences and formally surrenders his German passport at the consulate, hearing within weeks that his Berlin apartment has been searched, his sailboat confiscated, and his bank accounts frozen by the new regime he refuses ever again to set foot inside.
stops.quote: As long as I have any choice in the matter, I shall live only in a country where civil liberty, tolerance, and equality of all citizens before the law prevail.
stops.quote_source: Public statement on renouncing German citizenship, 1933
suggested_refs: Einstein's letter of resignation from the Prussian Academy of Sciences, March 1933
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Fölsing, Albert Einstein: A Biography

stops.name: London, the Royal Albert Hall, the last address in Europe
stops.campa: Sheltered for weeks in a remote hut on Roughton Heath in Norfolk under the personal protection of Commander Oliver Locker-Lampson, MP, who keeps armed guards against assassination, Einstein comes to London only once, in October, to speak at a packed Royal Albert Hall on behalf of scholars driven from Germany. Ten thousand listeners hear him thank Britain, as a man, a European, and a Jew, for its work of rescue, and warn that without the individual liberty that let a Newton or a Faraday think freely, there would have been no science worth the name at all. It is the last public speech he ever gives on European soil.
stops.quote: I am glad that you have given me the opportunity of expressing to you here my deep sense of gratitude as a man, as a good European, and as a Jew.
stops.quote_source: 'Science and Civilisation,' address at the Royal Albert Hall, London, 3 October 1933
suggested_refs: The Royal Albert Hall 'Einstein Meeting' of 3 October 1933, in aid of refugee scholars
sources: Royal Albert Hall archive, 'Albert Einstein'
Culture.wursten.be, 'Science and Civilisation' (full text)
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: New York, arrival without a homeland
stops.campa: The SS Westmoreland is met by reporters and a small crowd hoping for the great man on deck, but Einstein and Elsa, forewarned, are quietly taken off by tugboat before docking and land almost unnoticed, avoiding the spectacle he has come to dread. He carries no illusions of a temporary exile; Germany, in any recognizable form, is closed to him for good. Within days he is settled not in a great city but in the small university town of Princeton, New Jersey, where the newly founded Institute for Advanced Study has offered him, sight unseen of any campus at all, a permanent research position.
suggested_refs: Contemporary newsreel footage of Einstein's quiet arrival in New York harbor, October 1933
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Institute for Advanced Study archives

stops.name: Princeton, the Institute for Advanced Study
stops.campa: Abraham Flexner's newly endowed Institute for Advanced Study, with no students, no fixed curriculum, and no obligation on its members but to think, gives Einstein rooms first in Fine Hall and later in the Institute's own Fuld Hall, and a salary he need not earn by teaching a single class. He finds the small, quiet, tree-lined town almost comically self-important for its size, and also, after Berlin's mobs and Belgium's bodyguards, a genuine and lasting refuge; he will live out every remaining year of his life within walking distance of this same campus.
stops.quote: Princeton is a wonderful piece of earth, and at the same time an unbelievably ceremonious and academic little village of puny demigods on stilts.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Queen Elisabeth of Belgium, November 1933
suggested_refs: Fuld Hall, Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, Einstein's academic home from 1933
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Institute for Advanced Study, historical archives

segments.name: Princeton: the Bomb, the Bond, and the Unified Field

stops.name: Princeton, spooky action at a distance
stops.campa: With his young collaborators Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, Einstein publishes at the Institute a short paper describing a pair of particles that quantum mechanics says remain linked, however far apart they travel, so that measuring one instantly fixes the state of the other. He intends the argument, ever after called EPR, as a reductio: no sane theory of physical reality, he insists, should permit such an instantaneous, ghostly connection across empty space. Bohr's rebuttal satisfies the physics community far more than it satisfies Einstein, who goes on calling the effect, privately and for the rest of his life, spooky action at a distance, unresolved to his own satisfaction to the end.
stops.quote: No reasonable definition of reality could be expected to permit this.
stops.quote_source: Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen, 'Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?', Physical Review, 1935
suggested_refs: The EPR paper of 1935, source of the phrase 'spooky action at a distance' and of later quantum-entanglement experiments
sources: Physical Review 47 (1935)
Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Peconic, Long Island, the letter to Roosevelt
stops.campa: Vacationing in a rented cottage at Nassau Point on Long Island, Einstein is visited by his old collaborator Leo Szilard, who has come, with Edward Teller driving, to warn him that nuclear fission, newly discovered in Germany, might be turned into a weapon of terrible power before the Allies think to try. Einstein signs a letter, largely Szilard's drafting, urging President Roosevelt to fund American research into the uranium chain reaction before Berlin does; the letter, once delivered in October by the economist Alexander Sachs, becomes the seed of the Manhattan Project, though Einstein himself, refused a security clearance for his past pacifism, will never once set foot inside it.
stops.quote: This new phenomenon would also lead to the construction of bombs, and it is conceivable — though much less certain — that extremely powerful bombs of a new type may thus be constructed.
stops.quote_source: Letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Peconic, Long Island, 2 August 1939
suggested_refs: The original Einstein–Szilard letter of 2 August 1939, held in the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library
sources: Atomic Heritage Foundation, 'The Einstein–Szilard Letter'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Trenton, an American citizen
stops.campa: In the federal courthouse at Trenton, Einstein takes the oath of United States citizenship alongside his stepdaughter Margot and his devoted secretary Helen Dukas, who have made the same journey with him from Berlin. He keeps his Swiss citizenship too, unwilling to be stateless again as he was for five years after Munich, but it is as an American now, gladly and without ambivalence, that he will spend the war years advising the Navy on ordnance and buying war bonds at rallies, a stateless man's son become, of his own choosing, a citizen twice over.
suggested_refs: Einstein's certificate of United States naturalization, Trenton, New Jersey, 1940
sources: Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Institute for Advanced Study archives

stops.name: Princeton, Oppenheimer and the Institute made new
stops.campa: J. Robert Oppenheimer, fresh from directing the wartime laboratory at Los Alamos that built the weapons Einstein's letter had helped set in motion, becomes director of the Institute for Advanced Study, and the two men, so differently marked by the bomb, one who never built it and regrets the letter that started it, one who built it and cannot forget it, share the same small campus for the rest of Einstein's life. They respect each other without ever growing close; each, in his own register, becomes for the wider public the face of a physics that has learned it can end the world as easily as explain it.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Einstein and Oppenheimer together at the Institute for Advanced Study, late 1940s and 1950s
sources: Institute for Advanced Study archives
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Kai Bird & Martin J. Sherwin, American Prometheus (2005)

stops.name: Princeton, walking home with Gödel
stops.campa: For his seventieth birthday the logician Kurt Gödel, his closest friend at the Institute though almost his opposite in temperament, gives Einstein a paper proving that Einstein's own field equations permit universes that rotate as a whole, closing time back on itself so that a traveler could in principle voyage into their own past. Einstein, increasingly isolated from a physics community that has moved on to quantum field theory he distrusts, spends his last Princeton years chasing a unified theory of gravity and electromagnetism that never succeeds, and admits privately that it is the daily walk to and from the Institute beside Gödel, arguing without deference to either man's fame, that he now comes to the office for.
stops.quote: [He confided that his] own work no longer meant much, that he came to the Institute merely to have the privilege of walking home with Gödel.
stops.quote_source: Recounted by Oskar Morgenstern, colleague at the Institute for Advanced Study
suggested_refs: Kurt Gödel's 1949 paper on rotating-universe solutions to the Einstein field equations, given as a 70th-birthday gift
sources: Jim Holt, When Einstein Walked with Gödel (2018)
Institute for Advanced Study archives
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Princeton, the presidency of Israel declined
stops.campa: On the death of Chaim Weizmann, Israel's first president, the ambassador Abba Eban delivers Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion's offer of the presidency itself to the house on Mercer Street. Einstein, seventy-three, declines by return letter, pleading a lack of the natural aptitude and the experience for dealing with people that high office would demand, though the tie to the Jewish cause he names as the strongest human bond of his life remains unbroken; Ben-Gurion, for his part, is said to have worried aloud what on earth they would have done had the old man said yes.
stops.quote: I am the more distressed over these circumstances because my relationship to the Jewish people has become my strongest human bond, ever since I became fully aware of our precarious situation among the nations of the world.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Abba Eban declining the presidency of Israel, 18 November 1952
suggested_refs: Einstein's letter of 18 November 1952 declining the presidency of the State of Israel
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Offering the Presidency of Israel to Albert Einstein'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Princeton, the last signature, remember your humanity
stops.campa: Days before his final illness, Einstein signs, at Bertrand Russell's request, a joint manifesto with ten other eminent scientists warning that the hydrogen bomb now threatens the continued existence of the human species, and urging the world's governments to renounce war itself before some future conflict ends everything worth arguing about. It is his last public act, closing a life that began with a compass needle answering to a hidden force with a plea for humanity to answer, for once, only to its own survival.
stops.quote: Remember your humanity, and forget the rest.
stops.quote_source: Russell–Einstein Manifesto, signed 11 April 1955
suggested_refs: The Russell–Einstein Manifesto (1955), Einstein's last signed public document
sources: Pugwash Conferences archive, Russell–Einstein Manifesto
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe

stops.name: Princeton Hospital, the elegant departure
stops.campa: An abdominal aortic aneurysm, diagnosed years before and left deliberately unrepaired, bursts on the seventeenth of April; Einstein refuses the surgery that might prolong his life a little further, telling his stepdaughter Margot that he wishes to go when he wishes and to do it with some elegance. In the small hours of the eighteenth, alone with a night nurse who speaks no German, he says a few last sentences in his native tongue that she cannot understand and that no one afterward can recover; he dies before dawn. He is cremated the same day, his ashes scattered at a place he asked to remain unknown, and his brain, without family permission, is removed and kept.
stops.quote: I want to go when I want. It is tasteless to prolong life artificially; I have done my share, it is time to go. I will do it elegantly.
stops.quote_source: Reported final statement, refusing surgery, Princeton, April 1955
suggested_refs: Ralph Morse's photographic essay of Einstein's Princeton study on the day of his death, LIFE magazine, 1955
sources: Princeton University Press, 'The Final Days of Albert Einstein'
Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe
Denis Brian, Einstein: A Life (1996)
